label: Western cattle labor / cowboy work
description: Working culture of ranching, cattle handling, trail driving, horse labor, seasonal mobility, and wage work that underlay the later cowboy myth. Historical cowboys were ethnically diverse and their labor was more collective, skilled, and economically constrained than the later solitary gunfighter image suggests.

label: Mexican vaquero cattle & horsemanship tradition
description: Long-running cattle, horse, roping, riding, equipment, and vocabulary traditions developed in Spanish and Mexican ranching cultures and transmitted northward into U.S. cowboy practice. Terms and techniques later treated as emblematic of the American cowboy often have vaquero roots.

label: Black cowboy labor in the American West
description: Participation of Black cowboys, ranch workers, drovers, horsemen, and lawmen in western cattle economies after the Civil War. Their historical presence is substantial but was often reduced or omitted in later popular frontier mythology.

label: Indigenous participation in western cattle economies
description: Participation by members of multiple Indigenous nations in ranching, horse culture, cattle work, trade, and related western economies. This is not a single Indigenous tradition; communities had distinct histories and relationships to cattle, land, colonial states, and ranch labor.

label: Indigenous dispossession during U.S. westward expansion
culture: United States / Indigenous nations of North America
description: Treaties, warfare, forced removals, reservation systems, federal land policy, settler encroachment, and other processes through which Indigenous nations lost control of large areas of land during U.S. territorial expansion. This is a central historical structure of the frontier that later popular mythology often minimized or displaced.

label: Dime-novel frontier storytelling
description: Cheap, widely circulated nineteenth-century popular fiction that turned scouts, outlaws, Indian fighters, cowboys, and sensational frontier episodes into repeatable mass-market narrative types. Dime novels helped detach the imagined West from ordinary labor and convert it into portable entertainment.

label: Buffalo Bill's Wild West shows
description: Touring spectacles that staged buffalo hunts, sharpshooting, cavalry scenes, attacks, riding exhibitions, and frontier tableaux for mass audiences in the United States and Europe, converting contested western history into repeatable performance and iconography.

label: Game-show / elimination spectacle format
description: Media grammar built around contestants, rules, prizes, hosts, audience attention, elimination, escalating rounds, spectacle, and externally imposed incentives. The format predates reality television and can combine with later survival, streaming, and audience-participation conventions.

label: The Beatles — Hey Jude
description: Beatles song whose chorus survives as a fragment of cultural memory inside Stephen King's Dark Tower world. The reference is useful because King explicitly used familiar popular culture as a residue from a world adjacent to ours.

label: Late-Cold-War nuclear & ecological anxiety
culture: United States / transnational late twentieth century
description: Late-twentieth-century cultural anxiety around nuclear destruction, radiation, environmental degradation, species loss, ozone depletion, and technological power outrunning moral restraint. It is modeled as a broad context, not as a claim that any one issue alone caused a work.
